newsitem.title: USA: States can confine sex predators - U.S. high court.
newsitem.headline: States can confine sex predators - U.S. high court.

text.p: A closely divided Supreme Court ruled on Monday that states could confine dangerous sex offenders to mental institutions after they had served their prison sentences.

The high court upheld by a 5-4 vote a Kansas law that provides for the civil commitment of mentally ill sex offenders who pose a great risk of committing more crimes involving children if released into the community.

They held that the law, part of a nationwide crackdown on child molesters, did not violate constitutional guarantees of due process or protection against double jeopardy -- double punishment for the same crime.

"We hold that the Kansas Sexually Violent Predator Act comports with due process requirements and neither runs afoul of double jeopardy principles nor constitutes an exercise in impermissible ... lawmaking," Justice Clarence Thomas declared for the conservative court majority.

The ruling may affect similar laws in Washington state, Arizona, Wisconsin, Minnesota and California and possibly "Megan's law," a much-copied New Jersey law requiring public notice when a sex offender is released into a community.
President Bill Clinton signed a new federal law a year ago requiring states to tell localities when a convicted sex offender settles nearby.
The court's four most liberal members dissented, with Justice Stephen Breyer saying the purpose of the Kansas law was to inflict further punishment.

The case before the court involved Leroy Hendricks, 62, a convicted child molester with a long record of sex offences. A jury found he was a violent sex predator likely to commit similar crimes if released and ordered his confinement to a state hospital for treatment.

Hendricks' lawyer admitted he was likely to commit more sex crimes against children if freed but said predictions of future danger were insufficient to keep him confined, calling the law the equivalent of "effective permanent incarceration."
